title: Bhrigu and the five returns
hookLine: a son asks his father to teach him Brahman; the father gives him Hinduism's classic definition, then sends him away to find it
carry: brahman: what all is born from and returns to
tomorrow: "do not despise food. food is Brahman."
last: JOY GROWS AS WANTING FALLS AWAY.

lines: HE COMES BACK. HE'S SENT AGAIN.
cards: In the Taittiriya's third chapter, a young man walks up to his father and says, sir, teach me Brahman. His name is Bhrigu. His father is Varuna, and in the old hymns Varuna is a great god, guardian of the cosmic order.
If anyone could simply hand over the answer, it's him. He doesn't. He gives a few hints, then a definition with a hole in the middle, and then, more or less: go and work it out.
So Bhrigu goes. He comes back with an answer, and his father sends him away again. Five times, the story runs, and the father never once says, you're wrong.

teach.h: BORN FROM, LIVES BY, RETURNS INTO.
teach.b: Here's what Varuna gives him. First, a list: food, breath, the eye, the ear, the mind, speech. Then the definition.
That from which these beings are born, by which, once born, they live, and into which they go when they depart: seek to know that. That is Brahman. Born from, lives by, returns into.
So Bhrigu goes off and does tapas. Tapas is the word for heat, and for the heat of effort: discipline, concentrated thought. He comes back.
Food is Brahman, he says. After all, beings are born from food, live on food, and go back into food. Varuna doesn't argue.
He says: seek to know Brahman through tapas. Tapas is Brahman.
So Bhrigu goes again, and comes back with breath. Again, and comes back with mind. Again, understanding.
He's climbing the five layers of chapter two by himself.
The fifth time, he comes back with bliss. From bliss, beings are born. By bliss they live.
Into bliss they go. Anando brahmeti vyajanat: he understood that bliss is Brahman. And this time, the story doesn't send him away.
Two big Hindu teachings come out of this story. First, Varuna's definition: born from, lives by, returns into.

It became Vedanta's classic way to point at Brahman, and the Brahma Sutras build their second line on it. Second, the way of the guru. The teacher gives the frame and withholds the answer, and the student does the tapas.
Each early answer isn't wrong. It's a rung.

how: The third chapter of the Taittiriya, the Bhriguvalli, is chanted in Vedic recitation, and teachers often retell Bhrigu's five returns to describe how a student is led to find an answer rather than given it.

o: heat; the focused effort of discipline
a hint given by a father to his son
a gift a student brings to his teacher

games.q: Bhrigu's five answers — tap the pairs.

s: Varuna tells Bhrigu his early answers are wrong
he never says wrong. he only repeats: seek Brahman through tapas.
Varuna defines Brahman as that from which beings are born, live, and return
born from, lives by, returns into: seek to know that.
Bhrigu's five answers follow the five layers of chapter two

games.q: you're Varuna. your son comes back and says, food is Brahman. it's not the whole answer. what do you say?
o: seek Brahman through tapas. tapas is Brahman.
good enough. you can stop now.
games.why: Varuna just sends him back to tapas. Bhrigu climbs from food to breath, mind, understanding and bliss on his own.

practice: Take one question that matters to you, big, like what is all this for, or small, like what my friend actually needs from me, and say it once, silently.
Then don't answer it; hold it the way you'd hold something warm in both hands, and when an answer shows up, notice it, thank it, and put the question back in your hands.

wordCard.voice: Tapas, the heat of effort and discipline. Bhrigu is sent away five times by his father Varuna to do tapas, and he climbs from food to bliss on his own.

orig.note: Sanskrit tapas: heat, from tap, to burn; then the heat of effort, discipline, focused thought.

carryVoice: Your line: brahman, what all is born from and returns to. Bhrigu found it himself, the fifth time. Rest well.

sources.ref: Brahma Sutra 1.1.2 (janmadyasya yatah: that from which the origin of this world comes), traditionally read with Taittiriya 3.1
